messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

output:
Passes the repo's own slopwatch gate, clean. ~250 words:

---

At 3:14 on a Tuesday morning, checkout starts failing for about one customer in nine. Nobody gets paged. The error rate never crosses the threshold you set eighteen months ago, the dashboard stays green, and the first real signal arrives at 9:40 when someone in support forwards a screenshot from an angry user.

That gap — between when a system breaks and when anyone finds out — is what observability is actually about.

The word has been beaten half to death by vendors, so let me say plainly what it means. Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance: you decided CPU above 90% was bad, so you wrote an alert for it. Observability is the ability to answer questions you never thought to ask. Why are Canadian users on Android seeing four-second page loads, but only when the new flag is on, and only since Thursday's deploy?

You can't write that alert ahead of time. Too many combinations. The only way to answer it is to have kept enough detail about what your system was doing, per request, with the dimensions attached, that you can slice it after the fact.

Most teams learn this the expensive way. They ship, they grow, the architecture goes from three services to thirty, and then one Tuesday an outage takes six hours to diagnose because four engineers are reading four different log streams in four terminals and guessing at which one matters.

It didn't have to take six hours.

---

Draft is at `/tmp/obs.md` if you want to keep iterating on it. The one thing to check before publishing: the specifics are invented (the 3:14 timestamp, one-in-nine, six hours). Swap in a real incident from your team and the opening gets a lot sharper.
